I personally have my resume set up with Objective, employment history, education, professional organizations/certifications, and skills. The employment history and education should be with the most recent first. Under each job title, list some responsibilities. Make sure to use the same key words found in the job posting that you are applying. Same with skills, use the same key words. No need for months, just years of employment, and the graduation year for education. Try to keep it short and sweet. The majority of your stuff is going to be in the cover letter. Make sure you sell how you meet the basic qualifications first, so people will actually look at it. I was talking with a friend who in on a hiring committee, and 3/4ths of the applications are removed from consideration just from not showing how they meet the basic qualifications, because they focus so much on the desire qualifications.
I can't speak for your specific industry, but in most cases I would say to ditch the objective. Its clutter, HR already knows your objective is to pay your mortgage on time.

Almost every resume template I saw had this "Objective" section on it. I could not for the life of me figure out why everyone seemed to like that. My objective is to find a job to get paid. That's the whole reason I'm applying for a job in the first place and you know this. I ended up scrapping the Objective section because I found it pointless and a waste of space that could be used for my qualifications.
Absolutely agree. And if you have specific aims and objectives in the role then you can deal with that at interview.

Experience. Highlight experience. If you are building your CV for the future, get some experience in related fields.

Success. Find places where you have been successful and highlight that hardcore. Don't worry about what you suck at, exploit what you are good at. Its their job to figure out why they shouldn't hire you. Its your job to tell them why they should.

A lot of this is industry specific. You will probably get some better tips if you include what you are going into and where you are career wise.

It usually helps if you tweak it for the job you're applying.

If you think robots will read it, make sure you include key words from the job listing.

I prefer a single page for human read ones. I tend to talk most about the most recent things and downgrade the amount of space older things receive.
I just read through a bunch. Proper spelling and grammar are a must. I personally hate seeing large areas of white space, I say fill that page in.

[bulleted lists aren't working for me] As a hiring manager this is what I look out for: 1) Brief and to the point - 3 to 4 sides of A4 is fine. 2) Clearly sets out experience and qualification - focus more on detail that is relevant to the role. 3) No spelling or grammar mistakes. 4) I don't care about your other interests - I'm looking for work skills and a good fit with my team. 5) A well written covering letter - I want to see if you can write in an engaging manner. 6) Don't oversell - it's really obvious when applicants try to.

Relevant. Concise. No BS you think should be there because you watched the apprentice. Do not tell me you a re a motivated solutions orientated person. Stuff like that gets your cv in my shredder. I presume you have some motivation to apply, your drive and interest and motivation to take on the job need to come across in person.

Usually people in HR/Hiring Managers get a lot of resumes when looking for candidates, being very concise helps you stand out a lot -- I can tell you after reading 20-30 resumes, they all blend together at a point.

Try to design your resume for the job you're applying for, highlighting specific skills and experiences related to the field. You essentially want to have your resume represent what makes you the best candidate for the job with the least amount of text possible without needing to read your CV. In most cases, if your resume is good, the hiring manager won't even read your CV and book an interview with you. I've done this many times in the past personally -- I've even skipped through people who have Masters or Doctorates in their field because their resumes are so long that it seems like they're bragging. Hiring managers will also consider the culture of the group you're being hired into, if you're long winded and boring, that is taken into consideration as well. Also, if you're applying at a job fair, don't bring a CV at all, it's just more for the hiring manager to carry back to the office and will probably get shredded when it can't fit in the single iron mountain box they brought.

A CV on the other hand needs to be as verbose as possible, try to be as descriptive as possible with your past experience, even down to the exact process in some cases (generally technical tasks). However, in most cases CVs rarely get read.

One of the most common CV errors I come across is consistency. Be sure to stick to either present or past tense, and first or third person. Switching between the two is sloppy. Good luck with your job hunt!

One of the best resumes I ever got was one with a cover letter which showed that the guy really looked into our company policy, our motto, and showed a great amount of interest in our current projects.

There's nothing like someone who is genuinely excited about your company.

Depends.

If you're preparing a CV, larger is better. If it's a resume, keep it concise.

Places of employment will often have their own culture. That culture will include things like language, which is important. I have found it beneficial to read communications from the company closely, and watch for the language of this culture. You can then replace the appropriate words in my resume with these words in an effort to place yourself within that group. Most of the time it has a disarming effect and fosters good relations. It's similar to the way that some people fall into having a sympathetic accent when speaking to someone with different speech patterns.

Also be on the lookout for things like what sports/teams are discussed. When you've got your foot in the door in an interview, you should consider trying to find common ground in terms of interest and asking questions that influence the interviewer toward thinking that you'd be a good fit not only for the work itself, but the community of employees.

The page that appears allows you to change the sidebar, with the first text entry field. You want to use the second text entry field labelled "Custom stylesheet"

This is where you enter the CSS styling for the page.

After your CSS is there, you'll need to add this snippet of at the very bottom.
